languor

LANG-gur · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Languor is a pleasant, dreamy tiredness.

A comfortable languor spread through the cabin as the fire crackled and the storm raged outside.

Example

The days on the island slipped by in a warm languor, with no clocks and nowhere they needed to be.

This wasn't the draining tiredness of illness -- it was a relaxed, dreamy heaviness the travelers actually enjoyed, which is exactly languor.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

inertia: Inertia is a reluctance to move or change -- a stalled committee or a couch you cannot leave has inertia -- and it says nothing about how the stillness feels. Languor is a felt state: a warm, pleasant, dreamy heaviness in body and mind.

dreaminess: Dreaminess is a relaxed, unhurried drift of the mind, and a dreamy person may be strolling wide awake through a garden. Languor adds the body: limbs so pleasantly heavy that moving at all feels like too much work.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

energy: healthy vitality and liveliness

Where it sits · how deeply it slows you down

calm → languor → stupor

calm vs. languor: Feeling calm is simply an absence of stress; languor is a heavier, dreamier tiredness that makes you want to do nothing at all.

stupor vs. languor: Languor is a pleasant, relaxed heaviness; a stupor is a near-unconscious daze, usually far from pleasant.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together: Languor comes from Latin languere, 'to be weak or faint,' describing a soft, heavy weariness rather than exhaustion from real effort.

Use the root in a new word: languid: You've already met a word-family cousin of languor earlier in this course: the adjective languid (Part 1) comes from that exact same Latin root, languere.

Word Building

Word Choice

Unlike this unit's "lassitude" (a draining, often unwelcome weariness), languor describes a tiredness people usually find pleasant -- a lazy summer afternoon, a slow vacation -- and unlike "lackadaisical," it names a physical feeling rather than an attitude toward a task.
